title: The shadow that measured a world
summary: Eratosthenes could not travel around the whole Earth. So he let the Sun help him.

sources.title: American Physical Society: Eratosthenes Measures Earth

paragraphs.text: In the Egyptian city of Alexandria, a scholar named Eratosthenes wanted to know how far it was around Earth. He lived more than two thousand years ago, long before anyone could photograph our planet from space.
He learned of an unusual observation in Syene, far to the south. At noon near the summer solstice, sunlight could shine straight down into a well. The Sun was almost directly overhead.
In Alexandria at the same time, an upright object still cast a shadow. The same Sun was lighting both places. The difference held a clue.

Imagine two tiny sticks standing on a ball, some distance apart. Because the surface curves, the sticks point in slightly different directions. Sunlight arriving from far away meets them at different angles.

Eratosthenes measured the angle revealed by the shadow at Alexandria. It was about one fiftieth of a full circle. In a simplified model, the stretch from Syene to Alexandria therefore covered about one fiftieth of the way around Earth.
He also needed the distance between the cities. With that estimate, he could multiply by fifty to work out the whole circle. One small shadow had become a measuring tool for an entire planet.

The old accounts give the distance in a unit called a stadion. Because its exact length is uncertain, we cannot translate his result into one perfectly agreed modern number. The clever method, however, is clear.
He did not discover that Earth was round; other thinkers already understood that. He worked out a way to measure its size.
A shadow, a distance, and an idea were enough to reach beyond what one person could see. The world was vast, but it could be understood, piece by careful piece.
